articles.title: Trump agent’s ‘dead to me’ rant exposes ‘compelling’ motive in shooting: ex-prosecutor
articles.description: A former federal prosecutor said newly surfaced emails from a Trump immigration agent point to a motive in a deadly shooting. Joyce Vance, a former U.S. attorney, said Wednesday on her Substack show "Civil Discourse with Joyce Vance" that emails in which ICE officer David Brouillette told his sister she was "dead to me" amount to "strong, compelling evidence of motive" in the July killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine. Vance was joined by New York Times reporter Katie Benner, who reported with a colleague Wednesday that Brouillette's sister shared 2021 emails in which he lashed out at her Colombian partner, a man living in the U.S. legally. Benner's reporting also found Brouillette was brought on during the Trump administration's rush to staff up deportation ranks, and that his background report was not fully reviewed before he was put in the field. ICE has denied lowering its hiring standards and declined to confirm Brouillette fired the shots. Benner read one of the emails on air, which Brouillette sent after his sister asked relatives to record birthday messages for her toddler. "Tell your partner he can take his non-citizen a— back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries," Brouillette wrote. "You're dead to me, Liz. Enjoy it. Dead to me." Vance, who said she handled civil rights prosecutions during 25 years at the Justice Department, explained that cases like this hinge on intent. "What you have to be able to do is to prove motive," Vance said. "These emails and the testimony of family members established that this was not someone who had the capacity to look at the man he ended up killing and view him as a human being." "The fact that there's such strong, compelling evidence of motive, I think, makes this ripe," she added. "It should be a federal prosecution." Benner said a lawyer for the victim's family was told that Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey, whose term ends Dec. 6, plans to release public findings before he leaves. Vance noted Maine has its own civil rights law mirroring the federal statute. "We sometimes forget that prosecutors are human beings just like everyone else, and they don't like to leave unfinished business behind when they go," Vance said. Benner also flagged Dec. 1, when Brouillette's probationary year ends and firing him gets much harder. "So I'm really curious to see whether or not he makes it through his one year," she said. articles.title: GOP lawmakers snipe at each other as their final legislative plans fall apart: report
articles.description: Senate Republicans can’t agree on whether to use their final weeks in power to pass a party-line Pentagon funding bill, Semafor reports. The party’s remaining tool is budget reconciliation, which lets a bill clear the Senate without Democratic votes. Many Republicans want to use it to give President Donald Trump money to rebuild weapons stockpiles drained by nine months of war with Iran. But senators told Semafor they have no plan yet. Sen. John Kennedy (R-LA) predicted a plan would emerge, but said that for now he wouldn’t recognize it “if it jumped up and yodeled and bit me in the butt.” Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson (R-WI) said neither the White House nor leaders in either chamber have engaged with him, and that any push will have to come from rank-and-file members. Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD), who was reelected to his post this week, has repeatedly voiced doubt that the votes exist in either chamber. Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker (R-MS) and Sen. Jim Banks (R-IN) are pressing for a bill. Banks said it’s meant to supply the military, not fund the war. Sen. Rand Paul promised to vote no and said the bill would defy the election results. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO) questioned why Republicans would pursue it. Meanwhile, Sens. Susan Collins (R-ME) and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), two senators known for occasionally breaking with the party, have reservations about using reconciliation. Semafor reports many Republicans see the war as a leading cause of their midterm losses. It says frustration is also growing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who survived a House impeachment effort on Tuesday. Sen. John Hoeven (R-ND), who is close to Thune, said a party-line bill would give Republicans bargaining power with Democrats ahead of next month’s funding deadline. Other senators want to add provisions on living costs, elections and farm aid. Sen. Jim Justice (R-WV) said the party is trying to fit too many priorities into one bill, but that he may support it anyway. Reporter Burgess Everett notes the Senate has just four weeks of session left on its calendar, though Thune is open to adding time, and argues Republicans are already behind.
